title: Chuck Feeney’s Last Check
dek: In 1988 Forbes ranked him the 23rd richest American. He had already given the money away, secretly, four years earlier.

chapters.title: A boy from Elizabeth who sold everything twice

segments.text: Charles Francis Feeney was born on April 23, 1931, in Elizabeth, New Jersey, the son of Irish American parents scraping through the Depression. As a kid he shoveled snow and sold Christmas cards door to door. At 17 he enlisted in the Air Force and was sent to Japan with a signals intelligence unit, a posting that taught him two habits he kept for life: a taste for working abroad and a talent for keeping quiet.

The GI Bill got him into Cornell’s School of Hotel Administration, paid out at $110 a month, which did not stretch far at an Ivy. So he became the campus “sandwich man,” selling sandwiches to fellow students and fraternity houses. He graduated in 1956 with four months of benefits left and no plan for the degree.

Pay attention to the GI Bill. A government program paid for the education of a man who would later hand $8 billion to universities, including nearly $1 billion back to the school that took his checks. You will not find a better return on public money in this story, and the story has a few.

chapters.title: Fifty ships and nobody selling to them

segments.text: Feeney drifted to France to study at Grenoble, and there he met an Englishman trying to sell duty-free goods to American sailors docking at Mediterranean ports. In Barcelona he ran into Bob Miller, a fellow Cornell hotel-school graduate. The pitch was simple. Every serviceman leaving port was entitled to buy goods free of tax, and someone had to be standing at the gangway when he did.

The U.S. Sixth Fleet had about 50 ships in the Mediterranean in 1956, crewed by some 30,000 men. Feeney and Miller sold them tax-free liquor, then tax-free cars, which sailors paid for well before delivery. The business needed almost no capital and collected cash up front.
Any operator will recognize the shape: negative working capital, a captive customer, a regulatory gap. Feeney found the float before he found the product. Most founders get that order backwards.

chapters.title: The Japanese tour bus that built a fortune

segments.text: On November 7, 1960, Miller and Feeney registered Tourists International in Hong Kong and won the duty-free concession at Kai Tak Airport, trading under the name Duty Free Shoppers. In the spring of 1962, a Cornell friend in Honolulu tipped Miller off to an upcoming tender for the airport store. Miller flew in from Hong Kong and filed just before the deadline. The first full year’s minimum guarantee to the airport was $24,500.

Honolulu looked like a small bet on a market that barely existed. Japanese travel to Hawaii was in its infancy, and the few visitors who came faced punishing taxes on luxury goods back home. Feeney is the partner credited with seeing what that meant. He noticed that about 80 percent of Japanese travelers came in package tours, so DFS advertised in Japanese travel magazines and paid tour guides and bus drivers to bring their groups to its stores. It hired Japanese-speaking staff as the outbound wave built after 1964.

From there the map filled in: Guam, Saipan, Singapore, Anchorage, Los Angeles, San Francisco. Two minority partners, Alan Parker and Tony Pilaro, joined in 1966. By the mid-1990s DFS was distributing as much as $300 million a year to its four owners.
“I did not want money to consume my life.”
segments.author: Feeney, to Irish America

segments.text: By 50, Feeney had homes in New York, London, Paris, Honolulu, San Francisco, Aspen and on the French Riviera. Then he started dismantling the life those homes implied. He quit the clubs, bought clothes off the rack and switched to economy class. The famous plastic watch cost about $15.

chapters.title: How to disappear with half a billion dollars

segments.text: The trigger was mundane. In 1981, Feeney was thinking through a $700,000 bequest to Cornell. His advisers told him to set up a foundation to handle all future giving, and he did, in Bermuda, specifically to escape the disclosure rules an American charity would face. He lived on the island for a year to establish residency, and his lawyers persuaded the Bermuda legislature to pass a law letting the charity operate in secret.

Atlantic was founded in 1982. Its first grant created the Cornell Tradition, a program for students who work and volunteer their way through school. Then, in 1984, Feeney transferred his entire 38.75 percent stake in DFS to the foundation. Since nothing was sold, the stake had no market price. Estimates put it above $500 million. He never took a tax deduction for any of it.
In Dublin, Atlantic’s office went by a brass plate that read Tara Consulting. Grantees received money from a source they could not name, and Atlantic staff were bound by rules that kept it that way.

Here is the part that should stop any investor. Forbes ran a careful estimate of a private company, got the enterprise right, and got the owner completely wrong. Ownership was the one fact nobody thought to check, because nobody gives away a 38.75 percent stake in a cash machine and then keeps running the machine for free.

chapters.title: The lawsuit that would have outed him, so he outed himself

segments.text: Feeney wanted out of DFS. He wanted more cash flowing into Atlantic, and he believed the duty-free model had peaked. Talks with LVMH, the French luxury group, ran for about eight years, partly because two partners resisted selling. In December 1996 it bought out Feeney and one partner and took control of DFS.

Miller opposed the sale. A court fight would put the ownership records in front of the public, so Feeney moved first. In January 1997 he called two New York Times reporters, David Cay Johnston and Judith Miller, and told them everything. The filings put his share at $1.6 billion and showed it belonged to a Bermuda foundation that had been making anonymous gifts for 15 years. Atlantic emerged worth about $3.5 billion.
At the sale, Feeney set aside $26 million for some 2,400 of the longest-serving DFS employees.

He kept the secret through 15 years and a Forbes listing, and gave it up only when a lawsuit was about to give it up for him. Even the disclosure was a controlled exit. It was a very signals-intelligence way to go public.

chapters.title: Spend it while you can see it work

segments.text: Ireland came first emotionally. In November 1987 Feeney saw the aftermath of the IRA bombing at Enniskillen. His family’s roots ran back to County Fermanagh, the same county. He joined Americans for a New Irish Agenda, which shuttled between Northern Ireland and the Clinton White House pressing republicans toward negotiation, and he quietly funded loyalist groups working to stop the violence as well. Niall O’Dowd, who worked alongside him, says his biggest intervention came when Sinn Féin needed $1 million to open a Washington office and the process was on the line.

The bigger bet was the university system. Before Atlantic, Irish research universities ranked poorly; then Atlantic put €177 million into a national research program between 1999 and 2001 alone. As of 2014, $226 million in Atlantic grants had drawn $1.3 billion of government money into Irish universities. In 2012, nine universities on both sides of the border jointly gave him an honorary doctorate, something they had never done before.

Vietnam got $381.5 million between 1997 and 2013, much of it to modernize public and primary health care. RMIT’s Vietnam campus received more than $39 million to get started. Then came the AIDS clinics in South Africa, the cleft-palate surgeries through Operation Smile, a UCSF medical campus, earthquake relief in Haiti. In 2011 Atlantic made its largest single grant: $350 million to build Cornell Tech on Roosevelt Island.

Somewhere along the way Atlantic decided to spend itself out of existence. The staff did not wait for applications; as one Atlantic president put it, “we always approach them.” By 2007 there was about $4 billion left to give. By 2010 the endowment was $2.2 billion, with $5.4 billion already out the door. In 2012, at 81, Feeney had $1.5 billion left and a five-year runway.
“I want the last check I write to bounce.”
segments.author: Feeney, as quoted in Forbes

segments.text: The last grant went out in December 2016: $7 million to Cornell, for students doing community service. That closed the loop with the first grant, 34 years earlier, to the same kind of student at the same school. On September 14, 2020, Feeney and his wife Helga signed the papers dissolving Atlantic Philanthropies in a ceremony held online.

What he kept was about $2 million, enough for a rented two-bedroom apartment in San Francisco and the economy seats he insisted on. Bill Gates called him the ultimate example of giving while living. Warren Buffett, presenting him a Forbes 400 lifetime award in 2014, went further: “my hero and Bill Gates’ hero — he should be everybody’s hero.” Buffett has said Feeney was a cornerstone of the inspiration for the Giving Pledge, which he and Gates launched in 2010. Feeney signed it himself in 2011.
He died on October 9, 2023, at 92. Roughly 200 buildings he paid for stand on five continents. None of them carries his name.
“Try it, you’ll like it.”
segments.author: Feeney, to Forbes, at Atlantic’s closing

segments.text: Strip away the Bermuda law and the plastic watch and Feeney left a method, one that works at $8 billion or $80,000. Six pieces of it travel.

Set the end date first. Atlantic decided to spend itself out of existence, and planned every program toward a 2020 close. A deadline turns an endowment into a budget, and a budget forces choices. Perpetual foundations never have to choose.
Anonymity is a governance tool. Without his name on anything, nobody lobbied Feeney for naming rights and no grant was shaped to flatter the donor. Secrecy kept the question narrow: does this work?
Buy leverage, then walk away. In Ireland, $226M of Atlantic money pulled $1.3B of government money into research universities. The grant was the match that lit the state’s budget.
Go to the grantee. Atlantic didn’t take solicitations. Its staff went looking. Feeney ran philanthropy the way he ran DFS, by finding underpriced demand before anyone else saw it.

Fund institutions that compound. Buildings, universities, health systems. Cornell Tech and Vietnam’s public health system will keep paying out long after the foundation that funded them stopped existing.
Decide before the money gets loud. He moved the stake in 1984, when it was worth about $500M. By the time it was worth $1.6B, the decision had been made for twelve years.
The money is gone, which was the plan. The real test of Feeney’s idea is whether anyone else with a fortune chooses a closing date while they are still around to see it.
That chapter belongs to whoever is reading this, and it has not been written yet.
